newsitem.title: IRAN: Conservatives, centrists battle in Iran campaign.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives, centrists battle in Iran campaign.

text.p: Iran's conservative clerical establishment is fighting off a major challenge by a rainbow coalition of centrists and Islamist left-wingers as campaigning for Friday's presidential election enters the final stretch.

Supporters of conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri have plastered the capital with posters showing him with the late revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to portray their candidate as the man most capable of defending the values of Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution.

Mohammad Khatami, the other leading candidate, is backed by centrists close to outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wing intellectuals who accuse conservatives of trying to monopolise state power by adding the presidency to their control of parliament.

Khatami, a former culture minister with a reputation as a tolerant politician, has gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a stricter application of Islamic rules regulating everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression if Nateq-Nouri becomes president.

The economy -- specifically soaring prices and insufficient jobs -- is the campaign issue mentioned most often by electors weighing the merits of Khatami, Nateq-Nouri and outsiders Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri and Reza Zavarei. All except Zavarei are Shi'ite clerics.
The candidates have been stressing the need to fight social injustice and poverty in the wake of market reforms, but they have been vague on their economic plans.
In a television address on Sunday, Nateq-Nouri said he was committed to continued reforms but said the growth rate might have to be slowed down to avoid inflation.
"Inflation invariably leads to poverty so we should slow down the growth rate if it is necessary for providing social justice," he said.

Nateq-Nouri is backed by key clerical groups and is close to the bazaaris -- Iran's traditional merchant class of traders -- who worry that foreign investment in Iran would threaten their financial gains and political influence.
Khatami has also supported combining economic growth with social justice and opposed any return to a state-run economy as advocated by some of his supporters.
In a 30-minute radio address on Monday, Khatami said guaranteeing women's rights on paper was not enough.

"We have to see what opportunities are offered to women to achieve these rights. These opportunities are certainly less available to our women than to our men, and justice demands that access to education, to employment and to a social role be provided for women."
Faezeh Hashemi, Rafsanjani's daughter and a Tehran deputy who has championed women's causes, is actively campaigning on Khatami's behalf.
Nateq-Nouri, an ex-interior minister, leads a conservative group of clerics who with their allies have a majority in the 270-seat parliament.
Conservative deputies have slowed Rafsanjani's market reforms, but Nateq-Nouri's supporters say he would push ahead with them if elected.

Inflation was just over 23 percent in urban areas in the Iranian year which ended on March 20 compared with about 50 percent in the previous year -- a reduction that earned praise from the International Monetary Fund.
Unemployment is officially put at 10.7 percent of the workforce but this disguises high under-unemployment and the fact that many Iranians depend on income from at least two jobs.
